In [[number theory]], the '''Langlands–Tunnell theorem''' is a theorem due to [[Robert Langlands]] and [[Jerrold Tunnell]] that played a fundamental role in [[Wiles's proof of Fermat's last theorem]]. The theorem allows certain symmetries of [[algebraic number field]]s to be detected by the [[Fourier coefficients]] of [[modular form]]s. More specifically, it gives the [[modularity theorem|modularity]] of certain two-dimensional [[Galois representation]]s. In one common form, it states that every continuous, irreducible, odd complex representation
<math display="block">
\rho:\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/\mathbb Q)\to \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb C)
</math>
whose projective image is [[solvable group|solvable]] is associated with a [[modular form]] of weight one.<ref name="Langlands1980">{{cite book |last=Langlands |first=Robert P. |author-link=Robert Langlands |title=Base Change for GL(2) |series=Annals of Mathematics Studies |volume=96 |publisher=Princeton University Press |location=Princeton, New Jersey |year=1980}}</ref><ref name="Tunnell1981">{{cite journal |last=Tunnell |first=Jerrold |title=Artin's conjecture for representations of octahedral type |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |series=New Series |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=173–175 |year=1981 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1981-14936-3|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Motivation==

===Dihedral example===
In this context, modularity means that a Galois representation and a modular form give the same arithmetic data at almost all primes. A two-dimensional representation
<math>\rho:G_{\mathbb Q}\to \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb C)</math>
assigns to almost every prime <math>p</math> a Frobenius trace
<math>\operatorname{tr}\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_p)</math>. A normalized Hecke eigenform
<math>f(q)=\sum a_nq^n</math>
assigns to the same prime its Fourier coefficient <math>a_p</math>. The representation <math>\rho</math> is called modular if there is such an eigenform <math>f</math> for which
<math display="block">
a_p=\operatorname{tr}\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_p)
</math>
for all but finitely many primes <math>p</math>, together with the corresponding determinant character. For the Langlands–Tunnell theorem the modular forms are weight-one forms, and the associated Galois representations have finite image. The dihedral case is the easiest case of the theorem because the Galois representation is induced from a character of a quadratic field, and the modular form is an explicit theta series.

Let
<math display="block">K=\mathbb Q(i),\qquad \mathcal O_K=\mathbb Z[i].</math>
The rational prime <math>13</math> splits in <math>\mathbb Z[i]</math> as
<math display="block">13=(3+2i)(3-2i).</math>
Let <math>\pi=3+2i</math>. Reducing modulo <math>\pi</math> identifies
<math display="block">\mathbb Z[i]/(\pi)\cong \mathbb F_{13},</math>
with
<math display="block">i\equiv 5\pmod{\pi}.</math>
Now define a cubic character
<math display="block">\chi:\mathbb F_{13}^{\times}\to \{1,\zeta,\zeta^2\},
\qquad \zeta=e^{2\pi i/3},
</math>
by taking <math>2</math> as a generator of <math>\mathbb F_{13}^{\times}</math> and setting
<math display="block">\chi(2)=\zeta.</math>
Equivalently,
<math display="block">
\chi(r)=
\begin{cases}
1,&r\in\{1,5,8,12\},\\
\zeta,&r\in\{2,3,10,11\},\\
\zeta^2,&r\in\{4,6,7,9\}.
\end{cases}
</math>
This character is trivial on the images of the four units
<math>\{\pm1,\pm i\}</math>, since these reduce to
<math>\{1,12,5,8\}</math> modulo <math>\pi</math>. Therefore it defines a character of ideals prime to <math>\pi</math> by
<math display="block">\psi((a+bi))=\chi(a+5b\bmod 13).</math>
The condition that <math>\chi</math> be trivial on units is what makes this formula independent of the choice of generator of the ideal <math>(a+bi)</math>.

The associated two-dimensional Galois representation is
<math display="block">\rho_\psi=\operatorname{Ind}_{G_K}^{G_{\mathbb Q}}\psi.</math>
It is irreducible because <math>\psi</math> is not fixed by complex conjugation; conjugation changes the prime <math>3+2i</math> to <math>3-2i</math>. Its projective image is dihedral.

The corresponding modular form is the character-weighted theta series
<math display="block">f_\psi(\tau)=\sum_{\mathfrak a}\psi(\mathfrak a)q^{N\mathfrak a},
\qquad q=e^{2\pi i\tau},
</math>
where the sum is over integral ideals of <math>\mathbb Z[i]</math> prime to <math>\pi</math>. Since <math>\mathbb Z[i]</math> has class number one, this can be written explicitly as a sum over integers:
<math display="block">
f_\psi(\tau)=\frac14\sum_{a,b\in\mathbb Z}\chi(a+5b\bmod 13)\,q^{a^2+b^2},</math>
where one extends <math>\chi</math> by setting <math>\chi(0)=0</math>. The factor <math>1/4</math> accounts for the four units of <math>\mathbb Z[i]</math>.

Thus the coefficients are explicit weighted counts of representations of integers as sums of two squares:
<math display="block">
a_n(f_\psi)=\frac14\sum_{a,b\in\mathbb Z, a^2+b^2=n}\chi(a+5b\bmod 13).
</math>

For primes <math>p\neq 2,13</math>, this gives the expected dihedral trace formula. If
<math display="block">p\equiv 3\pmod 4,</math>
then <math>p</math> is inert in <math>\mathbb Q(i)</math>, and
<math display="block">a_p(f_\psi)=0.</math>
If
<math display="block">p\equiv 1\pmod 4</math>
and <math>p=a^2+b^2</math>, then
<math display="block">a_p(f_\psi)=\chi(a+5b\bmod 13)+\chi(a-5b\bmod 13).
</math>
This is exactly
<math display="block">\operatorname{tr}\rho_\psi(\operatorname{Frob}_p).</math>
So in this example the modularity statement is visible directly in the coefficients of a theta series.

=== Overview ===

The Langlands–Tunnell theorem is a bridge between two ways of attaching arithmetic data to prime numbers. On one side, a two-dimensional [[Galois representation]]
<math display="block">
\rho:G_{\mathbb Q}\to \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb C)
</math>
assigns to almost every prime <math>p</math> a matrix <math>\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_p)</math>, where <math>\operatorname{Frob}_p</math> is a Frobenius element at <math>p</math>. The trace
<math display="block">
\operatorname{tr}\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_p)
</math>
is then a number attached to the prime <math>p</math>.

On the other side, a normalized modular eigenform
<math display="block">
f(q)=\sum_{n\geq 1}a_nq^n
</math>
has Fourier coefficients <math>a_p</math> indexed by primes. To say that <math>\rho</math> is modular means, roughly, that these two prime-indexed sequences agree:
<math display="block">
a_p=\operatorname{tr}\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_p)
</math>
for all but finitely many primes <math>p</math>.<ref name="DeligneSerre1974">{{cite journal |last1=Deligne |first1=Pierre |author-link1=Pierre Deligne |last2=Serre |first2=Jean-Pierre |author-link2=Jean-Pierre Serre |title=Formes modulaires de poids 1 |journal=Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure |series=4 |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=507–530 |year=1974 |doi=10.24033/asens.1277}}</ref>

The Langlands–Tunnell theorem proves this modularity statement for odd irreducible two-dimensional complex Galois representations whose projective image is solvable. In less technical terms, it says that a large class of two-dimensional symmetries of algebraic number fields can be read off from the Fourier coefficients of weight-one modular forms.

One source of two-dimensional Galois representations comes from [[elliptic curve]]s. If <math>E/\mathbb Q</math> is an elliptic curve, then the action of <math>G_{\mathbb Q}</math> on the <math>3</math>-torsion points <math>E[3]</math> gives a representation
<math display="block">
\bar\rho_{E,3}:G_{\mathbb Q}\to \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_3).
</math>
For primes <math>p</math> of good reduction with <math>p\neq 3</math>, its trace is congruent modulo <math>3</math> to
<math display="block">
a_p(E)=p+1-\#E(\mathbb F_p).
</math>
Since <math>\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_3)</math> is solvable, the mod <math>3</math> consequence of the Langlands–Tunnell theorem implies, under the usual irreducibility and oddness hypotheses, that <math>\bar\rho_{E,3}</math> is modular. This residual modularity was one of the starting inputs in Wiles's proof of the modularity of semistable elliptic curves, and hence of Fermat's Last Theorem.<ref name="Wiles1995">{{cite journal |last=Wiles |first=Andrew |author-link=Andrew Wiles |title=Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's Last Theorem |journal=Annals of Mathematics |series=Second Series |volume=141 |issue=3 |pages=443–551 |year=1995 |doi=10.2307/2118559 |jstor=2118559}}</ref>

In the dihedral case, the relevant modular forms are theta series attached to characters of quadratic fields. Thus modularity can be checked directly from the coefficients of these theta series. The Langlands--Tunnell theorem goes beyond this elementary theta-series case by proving modularity for the tetrahedral and octahedral solvable cases as well, corresponding to projective images <math>A_4</math> and <math>S_4</math>. The icosahedral case, corresponding to projective image <math>A_5</math>, is not covered by Langlands--Tunnell because <math>A_5</math> is not solvable. Over the rational field, this case was settled by [[Serre's modularity conjecture]], proved Khare and Wintenberger together with work of Kisin. With this case covered, the [[Artin conjecture (L-functions)|strong Artin conjecture]] is known for all odd irreducible two-dimensional complex representations of <math>G_{\mathbb Q}</math>, including the icosahedral case.

==Statement==

Let <math>G_{\mathbb Q}=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb Q}/\mathbb Q)</math> be the [[absolute Galois group]] of the rational numbers. A two-dimensional complex representation
<math display="block">
\rho:G_{\mathbb Q}\to \operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb C)
</math>
is called ''odd'' if, for a complex conjugation element <math>c\in G_{\mathbb Q}</math>,
<math display="block">
\det(\rho(c))=-1.
</math>

One form of the theorem states that if <math>\rho</math> is continuous, irreducible, and odd, and if the image of the associated [[projective representation]]
<math display="block">
\overline{\rho}:G_{\mathbb Q}\to \operatorname{PGL}_2(\mathbb C)
</math>
is [[solvable group|solvable]], then <math>\rho</math> is modular. That is, there is a normalized [[cusp form|cuspidal]] [[Hecke eigenform]] <math>f</math> of [[weight of a modular form|weight]] one such that, for all but finitely many primes <math>p</math>,
<math display="block">
a_p(f)=\operatorname{tr}\rho(\operatorname{Frob}_p),
</math>
where <math>a_p(f)</math> is the <math>p</math>-th Fourier coefficient of <math>f</math> and <math>\operatorname{Frob}_p</math> is a Frobenius element at <math>p</math>.<ref name="DeligneSerre1974" /><ref name="Langlands1980" /><ref name="Tunnell1981" />

Equivalently, the [[Artin L-function|Artin <math>L</math>-function]] <math>L(s,\rho)</math> agrees with the <math>L</math>-function of a weight-one modular form. In particular, the theorem proves [[Artin conjecture (L-functions)|Artin's conjecture]] for such representations.
